client: I’ve been feeling really lonely since my partner moved abroad for work six months ago. We used to do everything together, and now it just feels like we’re drifting apart, even though we try to stay in touch. I’m not sure if therapy can really help with this—it’s not like it can change the distance between us.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a deep sense of loss and uncertainty about this change in your relationship. That distance—both physical and emotional—can feel especially painful when you were so connected before. What thoughts come up most often when you notice that feeling of drifting apart?

client: I keep thinking "What if they meet someone else there?" or "Maybe they don't miss me as much as I miss them." It's especially bad late at night when I'm alone with my thoughts. I know these worries are probably irrational, but they feel so real in the moment.
therapist: Those nighttime worries sound incredibly heavy to carry alone—it makes sense that they'd feel so vivid when the world is quiet and you're left with just your thoughts. I notice you used the word "irrational"—what makes you think these worries might not be based in reality?

client: Well, rationally I know my partner cares about me—they call almost every day and tell me they miss me. But I guess my anxiety just latches onto worst-case scenarios. It’s like part of me knows it’s irrational, but another part keeps saying "What if?" It’s exhausting.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught in a tug-of-war between what you rationally know to be true and those persistent "what if" thoughts—that can be really draining. When you notice these anxious thoughts creeping in, especially at night, what have you tried to help calm or challenge them?

client: I try watching TV or scrolling through my phone to distract myself, but that just makes me feel worse because I see all these happy couples on social media. Sometimes I text friends, but I don't want to bother them late at night with my anxiety. It feels like nothing really helps.
therapist: It sounds like you're caught in a difficult spot—trying to cope but feeling like nothing truly eases the weight of those thoughts. When you notice that scrolling or watching TV isn’t helping, what would it feel like to try something different, like jotting down your thoughts or practicing grounding techniques in those moments?

client: I guess writing things down might help, but I worry it'll just make me focus on the negative thoughts even more. The idea of grounding techniques sounds nice in theory, but when I'm in that anxious headspace, it's hard to remember or believe anything will help. Everything feels so overwhelming in the moment.
therapist: I hear how overwhelming it feels in those moments—like no tool or technique could possibly cut through the weight of those thoughts. That hopelessness makes sense when anxiety has such a strong grip. What if we tried something small together now, like a quick grounding exercise, so you’d have a clearer sense of it before those late-night moments hit?

client: I'm willing to try, but I don't think it'll do much. My mind always races back to worrying no matter what I do. How is noticing things around me supposed to help when the problem is thousands of miles away?
therapist: It sounds like you're feeling both skeptical and stuck—like no matter what you try, those worries keep pulling you back. That makes complete sense when the source of your pain feels so big and far beyond your control. While we can't change the distance, we can work on how those anxious thoughts affect you in the present moment. Would you be willing to try a quick exercise together, just to see what it feels like?

client: Okay, I'll try it, but I'm not convinced. I just feel like no exercise is going to change the fact that I'm lying alone in bed while my partner is living a whole separate life on another continent. The distance is the real problem, not how I think about it.
therapist: I hear how deeply painful this situation is for you—it’s not just about thoughts, but about the very real, physical absence of someone you love. That loneliness can feel impossible to soothe when the cause seems so fixed. Let’s try something simple together: name one thing in this room that’s a color you like. Not to fix the distance, but to help you feel a little more anchored right now. What do you see?

client: I notice my coffee mug—it's this soft blue color that usually calms me. But now I just feel sad looking at it because my partner gave it to me before they left. This is what always happens—everything reminds me of them and just makes the loneliness worse.
therapist: It sounds like even the things that used to bring comfort now feel bittersweet—like they're highlighting the absence even more. That longing can make everything feel tinged with sadness. When those waves of grief come up, what would it feel like to acknowledge the love behind that mug, rather than just the loneliness it brings now?

client: I never thought about it that way—that the sadness comes from love, not just absence. But it's hard to focus on the love when it hurts so much. Maybe I could try holding the mug and remembering our good morning coffee rituals instead of just missing them.
therapist: That’s such a thoughtful shift—focusing on the connection behind the sadness rather than just the pain of the distance. It sounds like those morning rituals hold a lot of meaning for you. What would it feel like to try that today—to hold the mug and let yourself remember those moments, even if it brings a mix of emotions?

client: I think I could try it, but I'm worried it'll just make me cry. I don't want to feel even more overwhelmed by the sadness. At the same time, maybe it's better to feel something than just numb myself with distractions every night.
therapist: It sounds like you're weighing a difficult choice—between letting yourself feel the sadness fully or keeping it at arm's length. That tension makes so much sense when grief feels so close to the surface. What would it be like to approach this gently—maybe setting a timer for 5 minutes to remember those moments, then shifting to something soothing afterward?
